problem: Prior DRL navigation work (e.g. Mirowski et al. 2017) reports only goal-finding time or reward, so it cannot say whether agents actually gather and exploit map information, and it is rarely tested on truly unseen maps.
motivation: Classical navigation splits exploration (mapping) from exploitation (planning). Whether end-to-end DRL agents implicitly do both determines if they can replace mapping pipelines. The authors build a staged benchmark with metrics that separate exploration from exploitation, so the two abilities can be measured directly.
key_idea: Evaluate NavA3C+D1D2L in a 5-stage suite that progressively randomizes spawn, goal and maze, using Latency-1:>1 and a new Distance-inefficiency metric, to test whether DRL agents exploit map information.
insight: With a static map the agent exploits map information (Latency-1:>1 above 1 for random goals) but paths are suboptimal (Distance-inefficiency above 1). With a random goal, random spawn and random map (train on 1000 maps, test on unseen maps) Latency-1:>1 is about 1 and Distance-inefficiency is large, so the agent only explores randomly. On the simple Square and Goal maps the shortest path is chosen only 50.4% and 42.6% of the time, which is chance level. Reward rises from 10 to 100 training maps but is flat afterwards, suggesting the agent learns an average exploration strategy rather than mapping.
method: Environment: DeepMind Lab random mazes (1100 generated by DFS); goal +10, apples +1, wall penalty -0.2; T=1200 steps; the agent re-spawns after each goal hit; textures are random.

Agent: simplified NavA3C+D1D2L with a CNN (16 and 32 filters), LSTM-256 and LSTM-64; inputs are the image, previous action and previous reward; auxiliary depth (D1, D2) and loop-closure (L) heads; trained with A3C.

5-stage benchmark: (1) static goal, spawn and map; (2) static goal, random spawn; (3) random goal, static spawn; (4) random goal and spawn on a static map; (5) random goal, spawn and map (train on 1000 maps, test on 100 unseen).

Metrics: Latency-1:>1 = (N-1)τ1/(τN-τ1), the ratio of first-find time to average revisit time. Distance-inefficiency = distance traveled after the first find divided by the sum of approximate shortest (Manhattan) spawn-to-goal distances.

Diagnostics: training on 10/100/500/1000 maps; ablating textures and apples at test time; two-path Square and Goal maps to check whether the agent picks the shortest route; gradient-based attention maps.

setting.backbone: NavA3C+D1D2L (CNN + 2-layer LSTM, A3C), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: RL in DeepMind Lab on procedurally generated mazes: 1 to 10 static maps, or subsets of 1000 random maps (10/100/500/1000); tested on 100 unseen maps
setting.observation: first-person monocular RGB 84x84 plus previous action and previous reward
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: move forward/backward, rotate left/right

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). The only numeric values in the text are the shortest-path rates on the Square map (50.4% ±12.8%) and the Goal map (42.6% ±35.1%), which are not on a standard benchmark.
results: When trained and tested on the same map, the agent exploits map information: reward is high for static goals, Distance-inefficiency is near 1, and Latency-1:>1 is above 1 for random goals. It does not transfer to unseen maps: Latency-1:>1 is about 1, Distance-inefficiency is high, and the shortest path is chosen at chance level on simple test maps.
limitations: Only one architecture (NavA3C+D1D2L) is studied, in synthetic DeepMind Lab block mazes, so the conclusions may not generalize to other DRL methods.
The shortest path is approximated by Manhattan distance, and the attention analysis is qualitative and gradient-based.
No fix is proposed; the paper only diagnoses the failure.
